sleepCycles.heading: Understanding Sleep Cycles
sleepCycles.sub1: Your body heals in sleep. Your brain organizes your future in sleep.
sleepCycles.sub2: Healthy sleep occurs in repeating cycles throughout the night. Each cycle lasts approximately <s1>90 to 120 minutes</s1>, and most adults experience <s2>4 to 6 cycles</s2> every night.
sleepCycles.nrem3: Tissue repair, immune strengthening, physical restoration
sleepCycles.rem4: Refreshes the mind, Cleans the junk memory
sleepCycles.band2: REM Sleep supports mental and emotional restoration.
sleepCycles.band3: Both are essential for optimal health and performance.

disorders.heading: Common Sleep Disorders - 8 Types
disorders.sub: Sleep disorders can affect sleep quality, daytime functioning, productivity, emotional well-being, and long-term health.

insomnia.title: Insomnia
insomnia.subtitle: Difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking too early despite having the opportunity to sleep.

osa.title: Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA)
osa.subtitle: Repeated interruptions in breathing caused by temporary airway collapse during sleep.

rls.title: Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS)
rls.subtitle: An uncomfortable urge to move the legs, often worsening during the evening and night.

circadian.title: Circadian Rhythm Disorders
circadian.subtitle: Disruptions in the body's natural clock, including shift-work disorder, jet lag, delayed sleep phase, and advanced sleep phase.

narcolepsy.title: Narcolepsy
narcolepsy.subtitle: A neurological condition characterized by excessive daytime sleepiness and sudden sleep episodes.

hypersomnia.title: Hypersomnia
hypersomnia.subtitle: Persistent excessive sleepiness despite adequate sleep duration.

parasomnias.title: Parasomnias
parasomnias.subtitle: Sleepwalking, sleep talking, nightmares, night terrors, and REM behaviour disorders.

bruxism.title: Bruxism
bruxism.subtitle: Grinding or clenching of teeth during sleep.

disorders.bottom: Not all sleep problems look the same. Recognizing the signs is the first step toward improvement.

q1.a: A chronotype is your natural biological preference for sleeping, waking, and performing activities throughout the day.

q2.a: The main chronotypes are commonly described as Lark, Eagle, and Owl, representing morning, intermediate, and evening-oriented sleep patterns.

q3.q: How many hours of sleep do adults need?
q3.a: Most adults generally need between 7 and 9 hours of sleep each night, although individual requirements may vary.

q4.a: REM sleep is a stage of sleep associated with dreaming, memory processing, learning, creativity, and emotional regulation.

q5.q: What is the difference between REM and NREM sleep?
q5.a: NREM sleep primarily supports physical recovery and restoration, while REM sleep supports learning, memory, creativity, and emotional processing.

q6.q: When should I seek help for a sleep problem?
q6.a: Seek professional guidance when sleep problems are persistent, affect daytime functioning, involve loud snoring or breathing pauses, or significantly affect health and quality of life.
